claim: The Kajabi 2024 Creator Economy Report found the median time from a creator's first piece of content to first earning £1,000 (converted from a US-dollar-denominated threshold without a stated exchange rate) in a single month is approximately 16 months.
stance_target: Time from starting content creation to first meaningful income is measured in over a year, not weeks or months as marketing often implies
scope_conditions: Kajabi (creator-platform vendor) 2024 report; no sample size (N) given in this secondary source; currency conversion from USD to GBP not disclosed, a possible distortion
quoted_support: The Kajabi 2024 Creator Economy Report found that the median time from first piece of content to first £1,000 earned in a month is about 16 months.
region: UK/US framing; currency in GBP; Western-only, no Southeast Asia data

claim: ConvertKit/Kit's data suggests roughly 60% of creators quit within their first 12 months, a period the same source states typically precedes when revenue usually begins.
stance_target: Creator attrition rate in year one is very high, and quitting largely happens before income has had time to develop
scope_conditions: ConvertKit/Kit (email-platform vendor) self-reported data; no sample size (N) given in this secondary source; population likely skewed toward creators who signed up for a creator-focused email tool, not a representative sample of all who attempt content creation
quoted_support: ConvertKit's data suggests roughly 60% of creators quit within the first 12 months
time_period: First 12 months of creating; 2024 vendor data
region: Western framing (UK/US); no Southeast Asia data

claim: The Influencer Marketing Hub's 2024 Creator Earnings Benchmark found roughly 48% of creators earn under $15,000 per year from their content.
stance_target: A large share of creators earn well below a full-time living wage
scope_conditions: Influencer Marketing Hub, a vendor survey; no sample size (N) disclosed in this secondary source; this appears to be the likely upstream origin of the 'over 50% earn under $15,000' family of figures circulating elsewhere in this research corpus
quoted_support: The Influencer Marketing Hub's 2024 Creator Earnings Benchmark found that roughly 48% of creators earn under $15,000 per year from their content
region: Not specified; likely US/Western respondent base given the survey source

claim: ConvertKit/Kit's 2024 State of the Creator Economy report found 78% of creators have no email list, a monetization asset the article's own analysis identifies as the single highest-leverage income driver.
scope_conditions: ConvertKit/Kit 2024 vendor survey; no sample size given in this secondary source; likely skewed toward creators already using or considering creator tools
quoted_support: That's why email is the single highest-leverage asset a creator can build -- and also why 78% of creators don't have one, according to ConvertKit's 2024 State of the Creator Economy report.
numbers: 78% of creators have no email list
region: Western framing; no Southeast Asia data

claim: The article, itself monetized through affiliate links to the exact tools and platforms (Kit, Beehiiv, Amazon Associates, Awin, Impact, Metapic, Teachable, Kajabi) it recommends as the solution to creator income failure, presents a thesis -- that creators fail from lacking monetization infrastructure -- that directly sells its own referral revenue.
stance_target: Reliability of the article's causal framing of why creators fail to earn money
scope_conditions: The Creator Insider, a UK affiliate-marketing content site; conflict of interest is structural (every named solution links to the author's affiliate account)
quoted_support: MATERIAL CONFLICT OF INTEREST: the page is monetised end-to-end with affiliate links to the email, affiliate-network, sponsorship and course tools it recommends

claim: The article presents an unsourced staged income timeline claiming creators typically remain near-zero income for 0-6 months, under £500/month for 6-12 months, £1,000-£3,000/month for 12-18 months, £3,000-£8,000/month for 18-30 months, and only reach £10,000+/month after 30+ months, attributed only to 'patterns we see across hundreds of creator income disclosures' with no dataset provided.
scope_conditions: Unsourced; attributed to the author's own proprietary, unpublished observation of 'hundreds of creator income disclosures'
quoted_support: Months 0-6: Building audience, testing what resonates, almost no income. Normal. ... Months 30+: The creators who survive this long -- which is a small minority -- often cross into £10,000+ territory

claim: HubSpot's 2024 Influencer Marketing Report found 64% of brands now allocate more budget to micro-influencers than macro-influencers, reversing a prior five-year trend, with a cited example showing a micro-influencer campaign achieving an 11x lower cost-per-acquisition (£25) than a macro-influencer campaign (£285) for the same brand and product.
stance_target: Shift in brand spending toward smaller-audience creators, relevant context for how income opportunity is distributed across creator sizes
scope_conditions: HubSpot 2024 vendor survey (no N disclosed in secondary source); the cost-per-acquisition comparison is from a single anonymised campaign, not a representative sample
quoted_support: HubSpot's 2024 Influencer Marketing Report found 64% of brands now allocate more budget to micro-influencers than to macro-influencers... Macro-influencer: 1.1M followers, 0.6% engagement, quoted £4,000 per Reel. Delivered 14 trackable sales. £285 per acquisition. Micro-influencer: 42,000 followers, 6.2% engagement, quoted £1,200. Delivered 47 sales. £25 per acquisition.
